text: Dozens of visual icons crowd that Visualizations pane, and it's tempting to just click whichever one looks the most impressive or sophisticated. That's exactly the wrong place to start, and it's a mistake that shows up in almost every beginner's first report. Here's the better approach — one that applies to every single choice you'll make across this entire chapter.

Start from the question you're actually asking, not the icon that catches your eye. Comparing values across categories? Reach for a bar or column chart. Showing how something changed over time? A line chart tells that story far better than anything else. Showing how individual parts make up a whole? Pie, donut, or treemap, depending on how many categories you're actually working with. Need exact values a viewer can read and compare precisely, side by side? That's a table or a matrix, and Lesson 53 covers both in full. And when one single number matters more than any comparison at all — total revenue, signups this month — a plain card is the right call.

Four questions settle almost every one of these choices in practice, every single time. First: what exactly am I asking? Second: how many categories does the data actually involve — a pie chart with two slices reads fine, but the same chart with fifteen slices falls apart instantly. Third: does the audience genuinely need exact numbers, or just a fast visual impression of the shape? And fourth: will this visual need to filter other visuals on the page, or be filtered by them — something nearly every visual can do, which Lesson 58 covers in full detail.

Ten lessons in this chapter build directly on this same decision process, one visual type at a time, from simple tables all the way to AI-powered analytics near the end. Get comfortable asking these four questions before you ever open the Visualizations pane, and the right visual practically picks itself. Next: tables and matrices — the visual for when exact values matter more than anything else.
